d3 — let's see if he falls into one of the traps. How should Black continue?

The reason it's not best is obvious: he weakens his kingside. After the bishop trade —

— look how nasty: he creates all these weaknesses on his kingside, which we exploit through targeted play and rapid development. The key word is rapid — if he plays the bishop to e2 and castles, the flame of the Stafford initiative is extinguished.
The knight takes e4 doesn't work here — we play the knight to g4, going straight after the e3-pawn; we don't let him consolidate. How can we pile up the pressure on it?
The queen to f3. Don't fall into queen-attacks-queen syndrome — don't play g5 just because it hits the queen; if you pose a threat, make sure it's meaningful. This one is —
— it forces the king up. Now, as many of you spot, if the knight were gone from g4 we'd have a pin —
— so the knight takes h2 comes to mind. In a classical game I'd play it — and it's too cool to pass up, so the knight takes h2.

— but this move is too cool to pass up, so we'll indulge; I actually think castling might have been even stronger.

— he actually escaped the pin, so don't forget to take the queen when the time comes.

The g-pawn recaptures. A clear application of 'strike while the iron is hot' — after winning material, your opponent often blunders more, less attentive to tactics. What tactical detail do we watch here? This rook — tactical observation 101.
The rook is unprotected. Is anything else undefended? The queen to e5 forms a classic triangle —
— a fork: not only do we win b2, we're going to take all the other queenside pawns.
Give me that, and that, and that — our king is perfectly safe, the game is over.

Assuming the rook to b1, and wanting to win efficiently, which pawn do we take? We can take c2 then a2 — could a case be made for a2 immediately? Yes, both create a passed pawn, but there's a subtle reason: if we play the queen takes c2, he walks the king to g3, opening his rook's defence and the queen x-ray.
So when we push the a-pawn, he might get his rook into the defence. Largely irrelevant — we're totally winning — but keeping the c-pawn alive walls his rook off from its defence.
That pawn on c2 sections the rook off from its defence, like plexiglas. Now —
— should we defend the a-pawn? No — push it. a4, a3 —
— and the game is over.
The knight to c4.
a3 — trying to make him give up the knight for the pawn. I hope he takes c7, because there's a very sexy winning continuation. And a big shout out to Eric Rosen, the king of the Stafford.
The bishop to h3. The queen takes c4 is the fancy move I mentioned, but it's not a good idea — the queen takes c4, the pawn takes c4, and a2 gets a little too fancy.

Be very careful — look at the whole board. Can he prevent the a-pawn queening? The rook to h1, and we'd only be up the exchange, starting over. When in doubt, go for the simplest continuation — the queen to a1 followed by a2 ends it, unless he plays the bishop to f5. Don't pre-move a2; stay vigilant of counterplay to the very end.
He plays the rook takes c7.

That forces a very desirable queen trade.
So investigate it, or take a look at my video for how to play against it. The point of c3 —
— is to prepare the move d4, slicing off the bishop's contact with f2 — that's the key, and it basically ends all of Black's counterplay; Black has very little compensation for the pawn.

So the Stafford is a good backup weapon; the bishop to e3 is inaccurate on this very account. But why shouldn't you make the Stafford your exclusive opening even if it works? Even if a gambit brings amazing short-term results, have at least one sounder opening, so you expose yourself to more positions and build a solid foundation. Offbeat players who reach 1700, 1800 then have to change their whole repertoire, having never played anything else.
